There are two ways of creating components, we can either do it in the CLI or we configure it in the Configuration file itself:

### 1. Specifying Namespace in the CLI
This can be done by specifying the name of the Namespace while applying the Config Map:

```
kubectl apply -f my-config-map.yaml --namespace=my-
```
Note that we have already created my-ns in the previous sections. Otherwise it would give us an error.

### 2. Specifying Namespace in the Configuration file
We can simply specify which namespace we want the component to be a part of it's configuration file. For that we can simply take our my-configuration.yaml file and edit it. We are simply adding the line "namespace: my-ns"

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
    name: my-configmap
    namespace: my-ns
data:
    db_url: my-service.database
```
Now if we apply it:

```
kubectl apply -f my-config-map.yaml
```
and if we check out our Config Map:

```
 kubectl get configmap -n my-ns -o yaml
```
We will get that same long output, but this would also include a line which says that the Namespace is now my-ns.
Changing the Active Namespace
The default namespace is our active namespace. In order to change the active namespace to any other namespace we can use kubens from kubectx. For that we will have to download kubectx by entering the following command

```
 sudo snap install kubectx --classic
```
now if we enter the command

```
kubens
```
we will get the list of namespaces present and the active namespace will be highlighted in green:
and then simply use kubens for changing the active namespace.

```
kubens my-ns
```
Now the active namespace has been changed to kubens. This means that by default if we do not specify the namespace the components will be created in the my-ns namespace.

title: Kubernetes Persistent Storage: Volumes, PVs, and PVCs
content:
Kubernetes provides different storage options for applications running inside Pods. Container filesystems are temporary by default, so data stored inside a container can be lost when the container is replaced.

## Kubernetes Volume
A Kubernetes Volume provides storage that can be mounted inside one or more containers of a Pod. Unlike a container's writable filesystem, a Volume can provide storage that is shared between containers and, depending on the volume type, can survive container restarts.
The behavior and lifecycle of a Volume depend on its type. For example:
- emptyDir provides temporary storage for a Pod.
- hostPath mounts a directory from the node's filesystem.
- Persistent storage can be provided through a PersistentVolume and PersistentVolumeClaim.
- CSI-based storage can connect Kubernetes with external storage systems.

### Types of Kubernetes Volumes
Kubernetes supports different types of Volumes depending on the application's requirements. Some commonly used Volume types are:
Volume Type	Purpose
emptyDir	Temporary storage shared by containers in a Pod
hostPath	Mounts a directory from the Kubernetes node
PersistentVolume	Represents persistent storage available to the cluster
CSI	Connects Kubernetes with external storage through CSI drivers
For production applications, persistent storage is generally managed using PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, and StorageClasses.

## Storage Integration
Kubernetes can integrate with different storage systems through storage plugins and the Container Storage Interface (CSI).

### Container Storage Interface (CSI)
The Container Storage Interface (CSI) provides a standard interface for integrating storage systems with Kubernetes. CSI drivers allow Kubernetes to work with storage provided by cloud platforms, network storage systems, and other storage providers.
Common examples include:
- AWS EBS
- Azure Disk
- Google Persistent Disk
- NFS-based storage
- Other third-party storage systems
CSI-based storage is commonly used with StorageClasses and dynamic provisioning.

### NFS Storage
- Network File System (NFS) provides network-based file storage that can be accessed by multiple systems.
- Kubernetes can use NFS storage through the appropriate storage configuration or CSI driver.
- NFS is useful when applications require shared file storage, particularly for workloads that need multiple Pods or nodes to access the same files.

## PersistentVolume (PV)
A PersistentVolume (PV) is a cluster-level storage resource in Kubernetes. A PV represents storage that can be used by applications independently of a particular Pod.
PVs can be:
- Statically provisioned by an administrator.
- Dynamically provisioned using a StorageClass.
A PV can represent storage provided by different backends, such as:
- AWS EBS
- Azure Disk
- Google Persistent Disk
- NFS
- Local storage
- Other CSI-supported storage systems
The PV contains information about the storage capacity, access modes, reclaim policy, and storage implementation.

### Usability
- Without persistent storage, application data may be lost when containers or Pods are replaced.
- PVs provide a separate storage layer that can be consumed by applications without requiring the application to know the details of the underlying storage system.

## PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)
A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is a request for storage made by a user or application. Instead of directly configuring a Pod with the details of the underlying storage, the application requests storage through a PVC.
A PVC can specify requirements such as:
- Storage capacity
- Access mode
- StorageClass
For example, a PVC can request:
- 2Gi of storage
- ReadWriteOnce access
- A specific StorageClass
Kubernetes then attempts to find or dynamically create a suitable PersistentVolume.

### PersistentVolumeClaim Access Modes
PVCs can specify different access modes depending on the storage system being used.
Access Mode	Description
ReadWriteOnce (RWO)	Volume can be mounted as read-write by a single node
ReadOnlyMany (ROX)	Volume can be mounted as read-only by multiple nodes
ReadWriteMany (RWX)	Volume can be mounted as read-write by multiple nodes
ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP)	Volume can be mounted as read-write by a single Pod
The available access modes depend on the storage backend and its Kubernetes storage driver.

## StorageClass
A StorageClass defines a class of storage that can be used for dynamic provisioning. Instead of manually creating a PersistentVolume for every application, a StorageClass can allow Kubernetes to automatically provision storage when a PVC is created.
StorageClasses commonly specify:
- Storage provisioner or CSI driver
- Storage parameters
- Reclaim policy
- Volume binding behavior
StorageClasses are commonly used in cloud and production Kubernetes environments because they simplify storage management.

## PV and PVC Working Together
PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims separate the storage provider from the application requesting storage. The workflow is:
- An administrator creates a PV or configures a StorageClass.
- An application creates a PVC requesting storage.
- Kubernetes looks for a suitable PV.
- If dynamic provisioning is enabled, Kubernetes can create a PV automatically.
- The PVC becomes bound to the PV.
- The Pod references the PVC.
- Kubernetes mounts the requested storage into the Pod.
This allows applications to use persistent storage without directly managing the underlying storage infrastructure.

## PV and PVC Lifecycle
A typical PV and PVC lifecycle can be represented as:
- Available: The PV is available for a PVC to use.
- Bound: A PVC has successfully claimed the PV.
- Released: The PVC has been deleted, but the PV may still contain data or require cleanup depending on its reclaim policy.
- Reclaimed: The storage is either retained for manual recovery or removed according to the configured reclaim policy.

## PV Reclaim Policy
The reclaim policy determines what happens to a PersistentVolume after its associated PVC is deleted.

### Retain
The Retain policy keeps the PV and its associated storage after the PVC is deleted. This is useful when the data is important and should be preserved for manual recovery or reuse.

### Delete
The Delete policy allows dynamically provisioned storage to be deleted when the associated PVC is deleted. This is commonly used when the storage should be automatically cleaned up with the application's storage claim.
Note: Recycle is deprecated and should not be recommended for new Kubernetes configurations.

## Creating a Pod YAML File with PV and PVC
In this example, the storage is created in three stages: PersistentVolume → PersistentVolumeClaim → Pod
The PersistentVolume provides the storage, the PVC requests that storage, and the Pod mounts the PVC.

### Step 1: Create a PersistentVolume
Create a file named my_pv.yml:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: mypv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 2Gi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data
```
Apply the configuration:

```
kubectl apply -f my_pv.yml
```
The Retain reclaim policy is used so that the storage is preserved after the PVC is deleted.
Note: This hostPath example is intended for a single-node learning environment.

### Step 2: Check the Status of the PV
Check the PersistentVolume:

```
kubectl get pv
```
To view detailed information:

```
kubectl describe pv mypv
```
The PV should initially show the Available status until a matching PVC claims it.

### Step 3: Create a PersistentVolumeClaim
Create a file named my_pvc.yml:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: mypvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 2Gi
```
Apply the configuration:

```
kubectl apply -f my_pvc.yml
```
The PVC requests 2Gi of storage with ReadWriteOnce access.

### Step 4: Check the Status of the PVC
Check the PVC:

```
kubectl get pvc
```
You can also check the details of the PVC:

```
kubectl describe pvc mypvc
```
The PVC should become Bound when Kubernetes successfully associates it with the PersistentVolume.
You can also verify the PV:

```
kubectl get pv
```
The PV should now show the Bound status.

### Step 5: Create a Pod Using the PVC
Create a file named my_pod.yml:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: my-container
      image: nginx:latest
      volumeMounts:
        - name: my-persistent-storage
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
  volumes:
    - name: my-persistent-storage
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: mypvc
```
Apply the configuration:

```
kubectl apply -f my_pod.yml
```
The Pod uses the PVC named mypvc, which is bound to the PersistentVolume.

### Step 6: Check the Status of the Pod
Check the Pod:

```
kubectl get pods
```
To view detailed information:

```
kubectl describe pod my-pod
```
The Pod should reach the Running state.
You can also verify the PVC and PV:

```
kubectl get pvc
kubectl get pv
```

### Step 7: Test Data Persistence
To demonstrate why persistent storage is useful, create a file inside the mounted volume:

```
kubectl exec my-pod -- sh -c 'echo "Persistent Kubernetes Storage" > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html'
```
Read the file:

```
kubectl exec my-pod -- cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
```
The output should be:
Now delete the Pod:

```
kubectl delete pod my-pod
```
Create the Pod again:

```
kubectl apply -f my_pod.yml
```
Check that the new Pod is running:

```
kubectl get pods
```
Finally, read the file again:

```
kubectl exec my-pod -- cat /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
```
The data should still be available because it was stored in the mounted persistent storage rather than only in the container's writable filesystem.

## Verify the PV and PVC Relationship
Run:

```
kubectl get pv
kubectl get pvc
kubectl get pods
```
This demonstrates how Kubernetes separates application storage requests from the underlying storage resource.

## Best Practices

### 1. Use StorageClasses for Dynamic Provisioning
- Use StorageClasses to automatically provision persistent storage.
- Avoid manually creating PVs for every application in production.
- Use the appropriate CSI driver for the storage platform.

### 2. Choose an Appropriate Reclaim Policy
- Use Retain when important data must be preserved after PVC deletion.
- Use Delete when storage should be automatically cleaned up.
- Avoid Recycle, as it is deprecated.

### 3. Request Only the Required Storage
- Define realistic storage requirements in PVCs.
- Avoid requesting significantly more storage than the application needs.
- Monitor storage usage regularly.

### 4. Use Appropriate Access Modes
- Select the access mode supported by the storage backend.
- Use ReadWriteOnce for workloads that require read-write access from a single node.
- Use ReadWriteMany when multiple nodes need shared read-write access and the storage backend supports it.

### 5. Avoid hostPath for Production Persistent Storage
- Use hostPath mainly for local development and learning.
- Use a StorageClass and appropriate CSI driver for production environments.
- Make sure the storage backend supports the application's availability and access requirements.

### 6. Monitor Persistent Storage
- Regularly check PV and PVC status.
- Remove unused PVCs and storage resources when they are no longer required.
- Monitor storage capacity and application usage.

### 7. Use Meaningful Names and Labels
- Use meaningful names for PVs, PVCs, and StorageClasses.
- Add labels and annotations where they help identify and manage storage resources.
- Keep storage configurations consistent across environments.

title: Kubernetes Secrets - Secure Storage for Sensitive Data
content:
A Kubernetes Secret is an object used to store sensitive information. Secrets help applications access sensitive data without storing it directly in Application code, Container images and Pod configuration.
- Secrets can be created separately from Pods.
- Pods can reference Secrets when they need sensitive data.
- Secrets can be exposed to containers through environment variables or volume mounts.
- Secrets are similar to ConfigMaps, but they are intended for storing confidential data.

## Use of Secrets
Kubernetes Secrets help manage sensitive information separately from application configuration. Their main benefits include:
- Separation of sensitive data helps keep credentials separate from application code and container images.
- Flexible access allows user to make sensitive data available to specific containers through environment variables or mounted volumes.
- Access control supports restricting access to Secrets through Kubernetes Role-Based Access Control (RBAC).
- Reusability allows multiple Pods to reference the same Secret.
- Simplified management supports updating credentials without rebuilding application images.

## Working
Kubernetes Secrets are API objects that store sensitive data as key-value pairs. A Secret can be referenced by a Pod and exposed to its containers when needed. The basic workflow is:
Kubernetes supports the following methods of making Secret data available to containers:
- Environment variables: Expose Secret values as environment variables.
- Volume mounts: Make Secret data available as files inside a container.
- Image pull credentials: Use Secrets to authenticate with private container registries.
- Application configuration: Allow applications to read credentials from mounted files.
Secrets are stored in the Kubernetes cluster's data store, etcd. By default, Secret data is Base64-encoded in the API representation, but Base64 encoding does not provide encryption.

## YAML Syntax
A Kubernetes Secret can be defined using a YAML manifest. The manifest specifies the API version, resource kind, metadata, Secret type, and sensitive data.
The general syntax is:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: my-secret
type: Opaque
data:
  username: YWRtaW4=
  password: cGFzc3dvcmQ=
```
The fields used in this manifest are:
- apiVersion: Specifies the Kubernetes API version. Secrets use v1.
- kind: Identifies the resource as a Secret.
- metadata.name: Specifies the name of the Secret.
- type: Defines the type of Secret. Opaque is the default type for general-purpose data.
- data: Contains key-value pairs whose values are Base64-encoded.
In this example, the values represent the strings admin and password, respectively.

### data and stringData
Kubernetes supports two fields for specifying Secret data: data and stringData.
Field	Description
data	Stores values as Base64-encoded strings.
stringData	Accepts plain-text strings that Kubernetes converts into the Secret's stored data representation.
The following example uses stringData:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: app-secret
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: admin
  password: my-password
```
The stringData field makes it easier to define Secret values without manually encoding them. It is a write-only convenience field and is not returned when a Secret is retrieved from the API.
Note: Base64 is an encoding mechanism, not encryption. Anyone who obtains a Base64-encoded Secret value can decode it.

## Types of Secrets
Kubernetes provides several built-in Secret types for storing different kinds of sensitive information. The type determines the intended purpose and, in some cases, the required data fields.

### 1. Opaque Secrets
Opaque is the default Secret type in Kubernetes. It is used to store arbitrary user-defined data, such as database passwords, API keys, and application credentials.
An Opaque Secret can contain multiple key-value pairs.
Example:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: database-secret
type: Opaque
stringData:
  username: dbuser
  password: dbpassword
```

### 2. ServiceAccount Token Secrets
The kubernetes.io/service-account-token type stores a token associated with a Kubernetes ServiceAccount. These tokens can be used to authenticate with the Kubernetes API server.
Example:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: service-account-secret
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/service-account.name: my-service-account
type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token
```
Kubernetes can populate this Secret with the associated ServiceAccount token and other relevant information.
Note: Manually created ServiceAccount token Secrets are generally not recommended for new applications. Short-lived, automatically projected ServiceAccount tokens are preferred for most Pod authentication use cases.

### 3. Docker Config Secrets
Docker Config Secrets store credentials used to authenticate with private container registries. Kubernetes can reference these Secrets through the imagePullSecrets field when pulling container images.
The kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson type stores registry authentication information in the .dockerconfigjson key.
Example:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: registry-secret
type: kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson
stringData:
  .dockerconfigjson: |
    {
      "auths": {
        "https://index.docker.io/v1/": {
          "username": "my-username",
          "password": "my-password"
        }
      }
    }

```
The Secret can be referenced by a Pod as follows:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: private-image-pod
spec:
  imagePullSecrets:
    - name: registry-secret
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: private-registry.example.com/my-app:1.0

```
The registry credentials are used by Kubernetes when it needs to pull the private image.

### 4. Basic Authentication Secrets
The kubernetes.io/basic-auth type stores credentials used for HTTP Basic Authentication. It typically contains a username and password.
Example:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: basic-auth-secret
type: kubernetes.io/basic-auth
stringData:
  username: myuser
  password: mypassword

```
The expected keys are username and password. These credentials can be consumed by applications that require basic authentication.

### 5. SSH Authentication Secrets
The kubernetes.io/ssh-auth type stores SSH authentication information, typically an SSH private key.
Example:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: ssh-auth-secret
type: kubernetes.io/ssh-auth
stringData:
  ssh-privatekey: |
    -----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----
    REPLACE_WITH_PRIVATE_KEY_CONTENT
    -----END OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----

```
The expected key is ssh-privatekey. Applications can use this Secret when they need SSH-based authentication.
The private key should be protected and made accessible only to the workloads that require it.

### 6. TLS Secrets
The kubernetes.io/tls type stores a TLS certificate and its associated private key. These Secrets are commonly used to configure HTTPS endpoints and secure communication.
Example:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: tls-secret
type: kubernetes.io/tls
stringData:
  tls.crt: |
    REPLACE_WITH_TLS_CERTIFICATE
  tls.key: |
    REPLACE_WITH_TLS_PRIVATE_KEY

```
The required keys are:
- tls.crt: Contains the TLS certificate.
- tls.key: Contains the corresponding private key.
Kubernetes requires these keys for a TLS Secret, but applications and controllers are responsible for using the certificate and key appropriately.

### 7. Bootstrap Token Secrets
The bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token type stores bootstrap token information used during the process of registering nodes with a Kubernetes cluster.
These Secrets are commonly stored in the kube-system namespace.
Example:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: bootstrap-token-abcdef
  namespace: kube-system
type: bootstrap.kubernetes.io/token
stringData:
  description: "Bootstrap token"
  token-id: abcdef
  token-secret: 0123456789abcdef
  usage-bootstrap-authentication: "true"
  usage-bootstrap-signing: "true"

```
Bootstrap tokens are sensitive credentials and should be given a limited lifetime and appropriate permissions.

## Using Secrets in Kubernetes Pods
A Pod can reference a Secret to make its data available to containers. The two common approaches are environment variables and volume mounts.

### 1. Using Secrets as Environment Variables
Secret values can be exposed as environment variables using the secretKeyRef field.
Example:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secret-env-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx
      env:
        - name: DB_USERNAME
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: database-secret
              key: username
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: database-secret
              key: password

```
In this example, the username and password values from database-secret are exposed as the DB_USERNAME and DB_PASSWORD environment variables.
A Secret can also be exposed through envFrom, which makes all its key-value pairs available as environment variables.

```
envFrom:
  - secretRef:
      name: database-secret

```
Environment variables are convenient, but they may be exposed through application diagnostics, logs, or process inspection. They should be handled carefully.

### 2. Using Secrets as Volume Mounts
Secret data can be mounted as files inside a container. Each key in the Secret becomes a file in the mounted directory.
Example:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secret-volume-pod
spec:
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nginx
      volumeMounts:
        - name: secret-volume
          mountPath: /etc/app-secrets
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: secret-volume
      secret:
        secretName: database-secret

```
In this example, the Secret is mounted at /etc/app-secrets. The container can read the Secret values from files named after the corresponding keys.
Secret volumes are read-only. When the Secret is updated, Kubernetes can update the mounted files eventually. However, applications must be able to detect and reload the updated values.
Secrets mounted using subPath do not receive automatic updates.

## Restricting Secret Access to Specific Containers
A Pod can contain multiple containers, but not every container needs access to the same sensitive data.
Kubernetes allows a Secret volume to be mounted only in the container that requires it. This follows the principle of least privilege.
For example, a Pod may contain:
- Frontend container: Handles user requests and application logic.
- Signer container: Requires a private key to sign messages.
The Secret volume can be mounted only in the signer container. The frontend container will not have the Secret mounted through that volume.
This reduces unnecessary exposure of sensitive data within the Pod. However, containers in the same Pod share a security boundary in several important ways, so container-specific mounts should not be treated as complete isolation.

## Security Considerations for Kubernetes Secrets
Kubernetes Secrets provide a way to manage sensitive data, but additional security controls are necessary to protect them.
- Values stored in the data field are Base64-encoded. Base64 only changes the representation of the data and does not prevent unauthorized users from reading it.
- By default, Kubernetes Secret data may be stored unencrypted in etcd. Encryption at rest should be configured to protect Secret data stored in the cluster's data store.
- RBAC should be used to restrict which users and ServiceAccounts can read, create, update, or delete Secrets. Access should be granted only when necessary.
- Secrets are namespaced resources. Applications should use appropriate namespaces to separate workloads and their associated credentials. However, namespaces alone do not provide sufficient protection without suitable access controls.
- Sensitive values should not be committed to Git repositories, even when they are stored in Kubernetes YAML manifests. Base64-encoded values are still readable by anyone who can decode them.
- Credentials should be rotated periodically and whenever they may have been exposed. Applications must be able to use the updated credentials.
- Secrets should be made available only to the containers and applications that need them. Avoid unnecessarily exposing credentials through environment variables, logs, or application output.

## Kubernetes Secrets vs ConfigMaps
Kubernetes Secrets and ConfigMaps both store configuration data as key-value pairs. The main difference is their intended use.
Feature	Secrets	ConfigMaps
Purpose	Store sensitive information	Store non-sensitive configuration
Typical data	Passwords, tokens, keys	Application settings, URLs, feature flags
Data representation	Base64-encoded through the data field	Plain-text values through the data field
Confidentiality	Intended for sensitive data, but requires additional security controls	Not intended for confidential data
Consumption	Environment variables or mounted volumes	Environment variables or mounted volumes
Secrets should be used for confidential information, while ConfigMaps should be used for non-sensitive application configuration.
Neither resource automatically provides complete protection against unauthorized access. Appropriate permissions and cluster security settings are required.

## Best Practices
The following practices help improve the security of Kubernetes Secrets:
- Protect Secret data stored in etcd.
- Use RBAC to restrict access to Secrets.
- Do not store plaintext or Base64-encoded Secrets in source control.
- Use short-lived tokens wherever supported.
- Replace exposed or outdated credentials regularly.
- Make Secrets available only to the containers that require them.
- Consider dedicated secret management solutions for centralized storage and rotation.
- Audit access to sensitive Kubernetes resources.

## Alternatives
Kubernetes Secrets are useful for managing application credentials, but other solutions may be appropriate depending on security and operational requirements.

### 1. External Secret Management Tools
- Tools such as HashiCorp Vault and cloud-provider secret management services can store and manage sensitive information outside the Kubernetes cluster.
- They can provide features such as centralized access control, auditing, and credential rotation.

### 2. External Secrets Operator
- The External Secrets Operator integrates external secret management systems with Kubernetes.
- It can retrieve sensitive values from supported external providers and synchronize them into Kubernetes Secret objects.

### 3. Secrets Store CSI Driver
- The Secrets Store CSI Driver allows a Pod to mount secrets from supported external secret management systems through a CSI volume.
- Depending on the provider and configuration, sensitive data can be made available without storing it as a conventional Kubernetes Secret.
- The appropriate solution depends on the application's requirements, security policies, and infrastructure.

title: Kubernetes - Kubectl
content:
Kubectl (often pronounced cube-control or cube-c-t-l) is the command-line interface (CLI) for Kubernetes. It acts as your control panel, allowing you to run commands against a Kubernetes cluster. Behind the scenes, kubectl is essentially a translator.
- It takes your command-line instructions, converts them into HTTP/HTTPS API requests and securely passes them to the Kubernetes Master Node (specifically, the API Server).
- From there, Kubernetes handles the creation, deletion, modification, or viewing of your resources.

## Kubernetes Internals
To understand kubectl, it helps to understand the environment it controls. Kubernetes orchestrates containerised applications using a Master-Worker node architecture:
- API Server: The front door of the Kubernetes control plane. This is the exact component kubectl talks to.
- Etcd: A highly available key-value store that holds all cluster data and configurations.
- Controller Manager: Maintains the desired state of your applications (e.g., making sure if you want 4 replicas, exactly 4 are running).
- Scheduler: Assigns newly created workloads (Pods) to available Worker Nodes.
When you type a command, kubectl authenticates with the cluster, sends the request to the API Server, and the API Server coordinates with the Etcd, Controller Manager, and Scheduler to execute your will.

## Architecture of Kubernetes Cluster
The Kubectl is a client-side tool that acts as a bridge between the users and the K8s cluster. It provides an interactive command-line interface for the users to run the commands with kubectl against the Kubernetes cluster.
The Architecture involves once the users/client executes a command through the command line it is authenticated with the master node of k8s Cluster through the Kubernetes API server. Based on the type of API request Kubernetes API server facilitates the orchestration and coordination of Kubernetes resources such as Control Manager, Kubernetes Scheduler, and Etcd resources.

## Installation of  Kubectl
You can setup the installation of Kubectl on any of the following sources of environment.
- Linux
- macOS
- Windows
Once you install Kubectl on kuba respective environment you can cross-check by running the below command.

```
$ kubectl version 
```
In the following screenshot you versioning details of kubectl:
To know more about of kubectl, please read this cheatsheet: kubectl cheatsheet
Syntax

```
$ kubectl [command]  [TYPE]  [NAME]  [flags]
```
- [command]: The action you want to perform (e.g., create, get, describe, delete, apply).
- [TYPE]: The Kubernetes resource you are targeting (e.g., pod, namespace, deployment, service). Note: This is case-sensitive.
- [NAME]: The specific name of the resource (e.g., my-nginx-pod).
- [flags]: Optional modifiers used to specify environments, output formats, or namespaces (e.g., -n my-namespace or -o yaml).
How to run the commands for resources that kubectl provides.

### Create a Resource Using Kubectl
In Kubernetes, a resource gets created inside a namespace which resource using which we can create other resources in a separate environment.
First, we are creating a namespace inside which we will create our Pod.

```
$ kubectl create namespace geeksforgeeks
```
We can create a Pod using the below YAML file.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
 name: geeksforgeeks
 namespace: geeksforgeeks
spec:
 containers:
 - name: nginx
   image: nginx:1.14.2
   ports:
   - containerPort: 80
```
The above file is a configuration file using which we are creating a pod of name geeksforgeeks in namespace geeksforgeeksnamespace which is an Nginx server. Similarly, we can create other resources like secrets, replica sets, etc by just changing the name in front of the kind and mentioning the key value in metadata and spec accordingly.

```
$ kubectl create -f geeksforgeekspod.yaml
```
The above discussed commands are implemented in the screenshot, try on implementing this

### To Get the Resources
Command to see all the namespaces.

```
kubectl get namespaces
```
To see the namespace geeksforgeeksnamespace run the below command.

```
$ kubectl get namespaces
```
Command to see the list of all pods.

```
$ kubectl get pods
```
This will show the pods in the default namespace. To list all the pods in a particular namespace we can pass the flag -n and the name of the namespace with `kubectl get pods` command.

```
$ kubectl get pods -n <namespace_name>
```
So if we have to list down the pod that we have created in namespace geeksforgeeksnamespace, run the below command.

```
$ kubectl get pod -n geeksforgeeks
```

### Describe a Resource
While get gives you a summary, describe gives you the deep technical details, status, and event logs of a specific resource. This is crucial for troubleshooting.

```

```
